title: Crochet buttonholes
subtitle: Working a horizontal buttonhole into a button band as you crochet
excerpt: A crochet buttonhole is a small gap worked into a button band by replacing a group of stitches with a chain, then working over the chain on the return row to close it. The size of the gap determines whether the button passes through cleanly.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: A crochet buttonhole made by substituting a short chain for a group of stitches, then working into the chain on the following row to form a stable opening.
A narrow strip of crochet fabric worked along the front edge of a cardigan or jacket to provide a stable edge for buttons and buttonholes.

content.text: A
chain-space buttonhole
is a small gap worked into a
button band

by replacing a short run of stitches with a chain. On the following row, you work the same number of stitches over the chain as you skipped on the buttonhole row, restoring the stitch count. The result is a stable, tidy opening.
What you need

items.name: A completed or in-progress button band
items.note: Usually at least 3 cm wide. A wider band gives more room for a neat buttonhole.

items.name: The button or buttons that will be used
items.note: Test the chain length against the actual button before committing to the band.

items.name: Stitch markers
items.note: To mark buttonhole positions before starting the buttonhole row

items.name: Crochet hook, to match the band

content.text: Sizing the buttonhole
The number of stitches to skip and the number of chains to substitute depends on the button diameter. A rough guide:
12 mm button: skip 2 dc (UK), replace with ch 2.
15 mm button: skip 2 to 3 dc (UK), replace with ch 2 to ch 3.
20 mm button: skip 3 dc (UK), replace with ch 3.

Always test by holding the chain loop open across the button before working the full band. The button should pass through with slight resistance, not force. A hole that opens easily will stretch further with wear.
Working the buttonhole
Plan the buttonhole positions and mark them with stitch markers before starting the buttonhole row. Space them evenly between the top and bottom of the band.
Work the buttonhole row: crochet to the first marker. Skip the marked stitches and work the chain of the same number. For a 2-stitch buttonhole: skip 2 dc (UK), ch 2.
Skip past the marked stitches and continue working the next stitch as normal. The chain sits over the skipped gap.
Repeat at each marked position. Work to the end of the row. (Stitch count remains the same.)
On the return row: work normally until you reach the chain. Work the same number of dc (UK) into the chain as the number of skipped stitches and chains. For ch 2: 2 dc (UK) into the chain space.
Continue to the end of the row. The buttonhole is now complete. Test by passing the button through.
Common problems

items.symptom: The button will not pass through the buttonhole
items.cause: The chain was too short for the button diameter.
items.fix: Rip out the buttonhole and rework with one or two more chains. Test the chain length against the button before closing the band.

items.symptom: The buttonhole stretches open and becomes too large with wear
items.cause: The chain was too long, or the crochet tension on the band is looser than the rest of the garment.
items.fix: Work the band at a slightly tighter tension than the body. A button that passes through with a little resistance will ease with wear but not stretch excessively.

items.symptom: The edge of the buttonhole looks ragged or uneven
items.cause: The stitches worked into the chain on the return row were not evenly spaced across the chain length.
items.fix: On future buttonholes, divide the chain length by the number of stitches to place and space them evenly. For a ch 2 buttonhole: 1 dc (UK) into each chain of the 2.

content.text: What to try next

Practise on a small swatch of button-band fabric before working the full garment. Work a strip about 5 cm wide and 20 cm long, place three buttonholes at regular intervals, and test each one with the actual button. The swatch also confirms that the band is wide enough to hold the button comfortably without pulling open at the edges.
